A federal appeals court further halted plans later on Thursday with an emergency order. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week.

The Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). "Public communication is essential to public trust," Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday. <?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<rss version="2.0" xmlns:media="http://search.yahoo.com/mrss/">
    <channel>
                    <title>Phys.org - latest science and technology news stories</title>
            <link>https://phys.org/</link>
            <language>en-us</language>
            <description>Phys.org internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.</description>

                            <item>
                    <title>What makes rock deep beneath continents break away and sink?</title>
                    <description>We usually picture mountain building as rock being pushed upward. But deep beneath some mountain belts and volcanic arcs, the opposite can happen: dense rock at the base of the crust can become unstable, break away and sink hundreds of kilometers into the mantle, dragging part of the rigid outer shell of the Earth (the lithosphere) with it. Seismic images suggest that this process, known as lithospheric dripping, has occurred beneath the central Andes and California's Sierra Nevada.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-deep-beneath-continents.html</link>
                    <category>Earth Sciences</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 23:20:01 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714409080</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/what-makes-rock-deep-b.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Device that measures strawberry skin's strength will aid breeders</title>
                    <description>Resilient strawberry varieties will be more easily identifiable thanks to a tool developed by University of Queensland engineering students. The prototype measures the strength of strawberry skin, a key breeding consideration for the Australian Strawberry Breeding Program at Queensland's Department of Primary Industries.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-device-strawberry-skin-strength-aid.html</link>
                    <category>Biotechnology</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 22:40:01 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714389857</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/strawberry-skins-stren.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Quantum software matches classical benchmark for a molecular interaction</title>
                    <description>Predicting how molecules interact is central to drug discovery: it offers important information about how a new drug might work in the human body, the side effects it can cause and more. Computationally modeling these interactions can reduce the need for lengthy and expensive lab work, but some interactions still remain beyond the reach of classical computers.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-quantum-software-classical-benchmark-molecular.html</link>
                    <category>Quantum Physics</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 22:00:01 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714409162</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/section-of-a-dna-stran.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>The call of the seamount: Two new armored tardigrades described in the Atlantic</title>
                    <description>An international team led by researchers from Senckenberg am Meer in Wilhelmshaven has described two new species of marine tardigrades. The tiny marine organisms were discovered in the sediment of the Senghor Seamount off the coast of Cape Verde. According to the researchers, the discovery underscores the role of undersea mountains as oases of biodiversity. The study, which includes comprehensive taxonomic descriptions of the new species, has been published in the journal "ZooKeys."</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-seamount-armored-tardigrades-atlantic.html</link>
                    <category>Plants & Animals</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 21:00:01 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714400952</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/the-call-of-the-seamou.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Broadening the role of RNA: A messenger, a mediator and now a condensate coordinator</title>
                    <description>New research about condensates—cellular compartments that act as hubs for facilitating biological reactions—continues to reveal novel insights into how cells function. Among those continuing to push the field forward are members of the Marine Biological Laboratory's condensate consortium, including Amy Gladfelter, a professor at Duke University and current co-director of the MBL physiology course, and former MBL physiology course student and past MBL Whitman fellow Dragomir Milovanovic, a professor at the Charité Berlin University Institute of Biochemistry.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-broadening-role-rna-messenger-condensate.html</link>
                    <category>Cell & Microbiology</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 19:40:01 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714399986</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/broadening-the-role-of.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>'Forever' chemicals? Don't be so sure, says engineer</title>
                    <description>Inside the disinfection room of Baltimore's Ashburton water filtration plant, 14 University of Maryland students clad in hard hats peered up at six towering vats of bleach used to treat water that flows from the distant Liberty Reservoir into the facility, killing bacteria and other pathogens before it's routed to the region's kitchen sinks.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-chemicals-dont.html</link>
                    <category>Environment</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:40:02 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714394429</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/forever-chemicals-dont.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>A fish as old as Montana—the blue sucker discovered to live well over 100 years</title>
                    <description>Using bomb radiocarbon dating on microscopic otoliths (earstones), researchers have found that a native species of fish in the Upper Missouri River in Montana is living up to 130 years—more than triple the previous estimate of around 40 years—and some blue suckers alive today hatched in the late 1800s, around the dawn of the automobile and when Montana officially became a state.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-fish-montana-blue-sucker-years.html</link>
                    <category>Plants & Animals</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:20:06 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714405002</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/a-fish-as-old-as-monta.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Caribbean corals are in crisis. Fossil reefs can help point to where corals may persist</title>
                    <description>The fossilized remains of ancient coral reefs often sit just meters from living corals in the Caribbean, where reefs have declined sharply over the past 70 years. Those fossils could help show where corals might survive a warming future. In two new papers, researchers at The University of Texas at Austin identify which coral species dominated ancient reefs in northeastern Jamaica and suggest how that record could guide reef rehabilitation.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-caribbean-corals-crisis-fossil-reefs.html</link>
                    <category>Ecology</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 17:00:01 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714403261</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/scuba-diver-swims-near.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Ancient bison hunting site in Texas challenges long-held assumptions</title>
                    <description>For decades, archaeologists questioned whether Native American communities in the Southern Plains hunted bison by driving herds over cliffs, a sophisticated technique widely documented farther north.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ancient-bison-site-texas-held.html</link>
                    <category>Archaeology</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:40:02 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714403142</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/a-bison-stands-against.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Scientists discover twist-tunable interlayer excitons in atomically thin anisotropic semiconductors</title>
                    <description>When light shines on a semiconductor, negatively charged electrons and positively charged holes—empty states left behind when electrons move away—pair up and bind together. This bound state is called an exciton. When two atomically thin semiconductor layers are stacked, electrons and holes can reside in different layers, forming what is known as an interlayer exciton (IE).</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-scientists-tunable-interlayer-excitons-atomically.html</link>
                    <category>Nanophysics</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:20:08 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714400028</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/skku-discovers-twist-t.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Gamified mobile payment features may drive adoption among Gen-Z users</title>
                    <description>Gamified features in mobile payment applications may significantly increase adoption among consumers in emerging economies, with men and women responding in almost identical ways, according to research published in the International Journal of Business Information Systems.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-gamified-mobile-payment-features-gen.html</link>
                    <category>Economics & Business</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:00:05 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714403801</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2023/mobile-game.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Record-setting X-ray laser reliably generates flashes with wavelengths shorter than distances between atoms</title>
                    <description>Researchers from DESY and European XFEL have demonstrated reliable production and transport of X-ray laser flashes with a wavelength of about 0.04 nanometers (or a photon energy of 30,000 electronvolts) at European XFEL, raising their own world record. This means that the X-ray's wavelength is much shorter than typical distances between neighboring atoms in solids, which enables the study of materials with higher spatial resolution than before.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ray-laser-reliably-generates-wavelengths.html</link>
                    <category>Optics & Photonics</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:00:01 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714403021</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/instruments-such-as-th.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Digital imaging workshop aims to reveal secrets in medieval manuscripts</title>
                    <description>Researchers recently used multispectral imaging technology to try to uncover hidden information from medieval manuscripts at the Rare Book and Manuscript Library at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. The library hosted a digital imaging workshop in early October that served as a pilot study for how the technology can help analyze fragile, centuries-old documents.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-digital-imaging-workshop-aims-reveal.html</link>
                    <category>Archaeology</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 15:40:09 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714400341</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/image-of-the-multispec.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>New hemp plant produces no detectable THC, potentially reducing risk of crop destruction</title>
                    <description>Scientists at Texas A&M AgriLife Research, a member of The Texas A&M University System, have developed a hemp plant that produces no detectable cannabinoids, including THC.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-hemp-thc-potentially-crop-destruction.html</link>
                    <category>Agriculture</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 15:40:01 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714400800</guid>

                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Tested on mushrooms, an AI model shows potential for detecting crop stress with far fewer computations</title>
                    <description>A new artificial intelligence (AI) model can detect stress in agricultural crops using a nondestructive imaging technique, allowing changes in crop health to be monitored over time. Developed by a team of researchers at Penn State, the new model shows promise for accurately detecting crop stress caused by drought, disease, nutrient deficiency and other causes while using less computing power than some existing AI methods.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-mushrooms-ai-potential-crop-stress.html</link>
                    <category>Biotechnology</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 15:20:11 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714402424</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/novel-ai-model-can-rel.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Can Instagram reduce prejudice? Study reveals the potential and limits of social media contact</title>
                    <description>A research team at the University of Potsdam has conducted a field experiment to investigate whether contact through social media can reduce prejudice. The findings suggest that following an unfamiliar Instagram profile for just three days can lead to more favorable attitudes—not only toward the group represented by the profile. The study was published in the Journal of the Association for Information Systems.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-instagram-prejudice-reveals-potential-limits.html</link>
                    <category>Social Sciences</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 15:20:09 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714400447</guid>

                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>A million tiny crystals reveal how semiconductors form distinct cores and shells</title>
                    <description>Perovskites and related materials called perovskitoids are promising semiconductor materials for solar cells, LEDs and light detectors. Their ingredients and internal crystal structures determine how they absorb and emit light. A chip just 2 centimeters across can hold roughly a million tiny crystals—becoming a miniature material library that can show how some mixtures separate into distinct cores and shells, changing the light they absorb.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-million-tiny-crystals-reveal-semiconductors.html</link>
                    <category>Analytical Chemistry</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 15:00:11 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714143916</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/chips-holding-a-millio.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Hazardous glacial lakes need reservoir-style safety oversight, says researcher</title>
                    <description>As the climate warms, thousands of glacial lakes are growing behind potentially unstable natural dams. Despite the potential risk of flooding to communities downstream, these lakes remain outside formal safety regulation.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-hazardous-glacial-lakes-reservoir-style.html</link>
                    <category>Earth Sciences</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 15:00:06 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714399840</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/hazardous-glacial-lake.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>People wade through floodwater because they underestimate danger—how to avoid risk</title>
                    <description>A footpath home disappears beneath brown water. The other side is only a few meters away and someone has already crossed. Turning back means a long detour and you will be late. Would you wade through? This is the kind of everyday decision that flood safety advice must address.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-people-wade-floodwater-underestimate-danger.html</link>
                    <category>Environment</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 14:40:06 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714396671</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/person-in-flood.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Global analysis reveals how lakes amplify glacier ice loss</title>
                    <description>Glacial lakes can accelerate the retreat of glaciers. If glaciers border a lake, the water can melt the ice from underneath; furthermore, chunks of ice can break off and fall into the lake. The extent to which these processes influence the situation, compared with other factors, had not been sufficiently clarified at a global level until now.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-global-analysis-reveals-lakes-amplify.html</link>
                    <category>Earth Sciences</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 14:40:01 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714399722</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/glacier-retreat-lakes.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>X-ray technique advances temperature measurements under extreme pressure</title>
                    <description>Scientists at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) have advanced the ability to measure temperatures in materials subjected to extreme pressures at the National Ignition Facility (NIF), providing new insights into how materials behave under conditions relevant to national security and high-energy-density physics.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ray-technique-advances-temperature-extreme.html</link>
                    <category>General Physics</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 14:20:06 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714399362</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/nif-x-ray-technique-ad.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Parasite protein expands understanding of how mitochondria build their ribosomes</title>
                    <description>Mitochondria are essential components of the cells of most organisms, including humans. They are often referred to as the cell's powerhouses because they produce the energy needed for cellular functions. However, mitochondria originally evolved from free-living bacteria that were engulfed by other cells in the distant past.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-parasite-protein-mitochondria-ribosomes.html</link>
                    <category>Cell & Microbiology</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 14:20:01 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714396301</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2025/mitochondria.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Mapping the microbes' arms race with viruses at planetary scale</title>
                    <description>Microbiomes are complex ecosystems, in which bacteria and archaea are constantly interacting with, and infected by, viruses. These viruses can significantly impact microbiome processes, not only by killing their host but also sometimes by temporarily providing additional capabilities to their host. As many viruses have not been grown in a lab, connecting them to their natural hosts has been difficult. A new bioinformatics toolkit and database are now available to help researchers make those associations at an unprecedented scale.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-microbes-arms-viruses-planetary-scale.html</link>
                    <category>Cell & Microbiology</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 14:00:27 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714397322</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/mapping-the-microbes-a.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>El Niño created a skiers' paradise in Chile—now it's Sierra Nevada and southern Rockies' turn</title>
                    <description>El Niño has a reputation for being a skier's dream, bringing lots of snow to California's Sierra Nevada and the southern Rockies. Tahoe-area resorts were already seeing the effects in mid-November 2026 as several feet of snow fell and some resorts prepared to open early for the season. But El Niño's supercharged precipitation can spell trouble, too.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-el-nio-skiers-paradise-chile.html</link>
                    <category>Environment</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 14:00:02 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714395537</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/skiers.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Practical organ-on-a-chip platform helps assess the toxicity of environmental chemicals</title>
                    <description>Among the thousands of chemicals used in daily life, toxicity information is available for only a small fraction. Much of this information comes from high-dose animal studies, which are costly, time-consuming and limited by species differences.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-chip-platform-toxicity-environmental-chemicals.html</link>
                    <category>Environment</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 13:40:06 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714395401</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/seoultech-researchers-2.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>New sources of neurotoxin linked to algal blooms uncovered in Florida and Kansas</title>
                    <description>Researchers have identified two previously unreported strains of freshwater cyanobacteria capable of producing a potent neurotoxin that poses risks to people, pets, wildlife and water resources and that some scientists suspect may have contributed to previous animal deaths.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-sources-neurotoxin-linked-algal-blooms.html</link>
                    <category>Environment</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 13:40:01 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714396541</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/algal-blooms.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Bumblebees challenge long-held beliefs about brain size and intelligence</title>
                    <description>Bigger brains mean greater intelligence, or so conventional wisdom goes. After all, humans have much larger brains than most other animals and are generally considered the planet's most intelligent species.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-bumblebees-held-beliefs-brain-size.html</link>
                    <category>Plants & Animals</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 13:30:05 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714401187</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/bumblebees-challenge-l.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Is it genuine love—or obsessive passion? Kierkegaard, the father of existentialism, had some thoughts</title>
                    <description>Young love, honeymoon love, infatuation—these often feel spectacular. You have a burning need to be in constant contact, and you don't want to let that person out of your sight.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-genuine-obsessive-passion-kierkegaard-father.html</link>
                    <category>Social Sciences</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 13:20:11 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714395173</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/a-painting-in-dark-col.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Clean energy choices shape environmental impacts beyond greenhouse gas emissions</title>
                    <description>The burning of fossil fuels such as coal, gas and oil is the primary driver of climate change, but clean energy strategies to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions do not systematically alleviate other environmental problems. In fact, some pathways add pressure on natural resources like land, water and minerals.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-energy-choices-environmental-impacts-greenhouse.html</link>
                    <category>Environment</category>                    <pubDate>Fri, 20 Nov 2026 13:20:03 EST</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news714395521</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/decarbonization.jpg" width="90" height="90" />

                    <title>Witnessing generosity from low-income donors more likely to elicit giving from observers, research finds</title>
                    <description>Billionaire Warren Buffett announced this month he will donate $5.47 billion to four foundations associated with his family ahead of Thanksgiving.                     <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-11-witnessing-generosity-income-donors-elicit.html</link>

items.title: What makes rock deep beneath continents break away and sink?
items.summary: We usually picture mountain building as rock being pushed upward. But deep beneath some mountain belts and volcanic arcs, the opposite can happen: dense rock at the base of the crust can become unstable, break away and sink hundreds of kilometers into the mantle, dragging part of the rigid outer shell of the Earth (the lithosphere) with it. Seismic images suggest that this process, known as lithospheric dripping, has occurred beneath the central Andes and California's Sierra Nevada.

items.title: Device that measures strawberry skin's strength will aid breeders
items.summary: Resilient strawberry varieties will be more easily identifiable thanks to a tool developed by University of Queensland engineering students. The prototype measures the strength of strawberry skin, a key breeding consideration for the Australian Strawberry Breeding Program at Queensland's Department of Primary Industries.

items.title: Quantum software matches classical benchmark for a molecular interaction
items.summary: Predicting how molecules interact is central to drug discovery: it offers important information about how a new drug might work in the human body, the side effects it can cause and more. Computationally modeling these interactions can reduce the need for lengthy and expensive lab work, but some interactions still remain beyond the reach of classical computers.

items.title: The call of the seamount: Two new armored tardigrades described in the Atlantic
items.summary: An international team led by researchers from Senckenberg am Meer in Wilhelmshaven has described two new species of marine tardigrades. The tiny marine organisms were discovered in the sediment of the Senghor Seamount off the coast of Cape Verde. According to the researchers, the discovery underscores the role of undersea mountains as oases of biodiversity. The study, which includes comprehensive taxonomic descriptions of the new species, has been published in the journal "ZooKeys."

items.title: Broadening the role of RNA: A messenger, a mediator and now a condensate coordinator
items.summary: New research about condensates—cellular compartments that act as hubs for facilitating biological reactions—continues to reveal novel insights into how cells function. Among those continuing to push the field forward are members of the Marine Biological Laboratory's condensate consortium, including Amy Gladfelter, a professor at Duke University and current co-director of the MBL physiology course, and former MBL physiology course student and past MBL Whitman fellow Dragomir Milovanovic, a professor at the Charité Berlin University Institute of Biochemistry.

items.title: 'Forever' chemicals? Don't be so sure, says engineer
items.summary: Inside the disinfection room of Baltimore's Ashburton water filtration plant, 14 University of Maryland students clad in hard hats peered up at six towering vats of bleach used to treat water that flows from the distant Liberty Reservoir into the facility, killing bacteria and other pathogens before it's routed to the region's kitchen sinks.

items.title: A fish as old as Montana—the blue sucker discovered to live well over 100 years
items.summary: Using bomb radiocarbon dating on microscopic otoliths (earstones), researchers have found that a native species of fish in the Upper Missouri River in Montana is living up to 130 years—more than triple the previous estimate of around 40 years—and some blue suckers alive today hatched in the late 1800s, around the dawn of the automobile and when Montana officially became a state.

items.title: Caribbean corals are in crisis. Fossil reefs can help point to where corals may persist
items.summary: The fossilized remains of ancient coral reefs often sit just meters from living corals in the Caribbean, where reefs have declined sharply over the past 70 years. Those fossils could help show where corals might survive a warming future. In two new papers, researchers at The University of Texas at Austin identify which coral species dominated ancient reefs in northeastern Jamaica and suggest how that record could guide reef rehabilitation.

items.title: Ancient bison hunting site in Texas challenges long-held assumptions
items.summary: For decades, archaeologists questioned whether Native American communities in the Southern Plains hunted bison by driving herds over cliffs, a sophisticated technique widely documented farther north.

items.title: Scientists discover twist-tunable interlayer excitons in atomically thin anisotropic semiconductors
items.summary: When light shines on a semiconductor, negatively charged electrons and positively charged holes—empty states left behind when electrons move away—pair up and bind together. This bound state is called an exciton. When two atomically thin semiconductor layers are stacked, electrons and holes can reside in different layers, forming what is known as an interlayer exciton (IE).

items.title: Gamified mobile payment features may drive adoption among Gen-Z users
items.summary: Gamified features in mobile payment applications may significantly increase adoption among consumers in emerging economies, with men and women responding in almost identical ways, according to research published in the International Journal of Business Information Systems.

items.title: Record-setting X-ray laser reliably generates flashes with wavelengths shorter than distances between atoms
items.summary: Researchers from DESY and European XFEL have demonstrated reliable production and transport of X-ray laser flashes with a wavelength of about 0.04 nanometers (or a photon energy of 30,000 electronvolts) at European XFEL, raising their own world record. This means that the X-ray's wavelength is much shorter than typical distances between neighboring atoms in solids, which enables the study of materials with higher spatial resolution than before.

items.title: Digital imaging workshop aims to reveal secrets in medieval manuscripts
items.summary: Researchers recently used multispectral imaging technology to try to uncover hidden information from medieval manuscripts at the Rare Book and Manuscript Library at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. The library hosted a digital imaging workshop in early October that served as a pilot study for how the technology can help analyze fragile, centuries-old documents.

Atlas Obscura - Latest Articles and Places New wonders and curiosities added to the Atlas. https://www.atlasobscura.com en-us Alta Rock Carvings in Alta, Norway Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:00:00 -0500 https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/alta-rock-carvings https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/alta-rock-carvings

One of the most extraordinary attractions in northern Norway is Alta Museum's outdoor area, where thousands of prehistoric carvings can be found. These are not paintings or replicas displayed behind glass – they are original artworks carved directly into the bedrock by people thousands of years ago. 

Some of the carvings date back more than 7,000 years, making them among the oldest and most significant examples of prehistoric rock art in Northern Europe. They depict reindeer, bears, elk, fish, whales, boats, hunting scenes, fishing activities, human figures and mysterious rituals. The carvings were originally made near the shoreline, and as the land gradually rose after the last Ice Age, new rock surfaces became available for successive generations of artists.

Light plays an important role in discovering the carvings. Depending on the direction and angle of the sunlight, the engraved lines can become much more visible or almost disappear completely. Low-angle sunlight, especially in the morning or evening, creates small shadows inside the carved grooves, making the figures stand out more clearly.

Some of the carvings have been painted red to make them easier to see. This red colour is not original to the carvings, but was added in 1970s to help visitors recognise their shapes and details. Today, the focus is on protecting the original rock carvings while keeping modern alterations to a minimum. As part of this conservation work, the red paint is gradually being removed to preserve the site's authenticity

The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognised in 1985 for its outstanding cultural and historical importance.

]]> ancient stone petroglyphs Shrine of the Most Blessed Sacrement in Hanceville, Alabama Fri, 20 Nov 2026 14:00:00 -0500 https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/shrine-of-the-most-blessed-sacrement https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/shrine-of-the-most-blessed-sacrement

Extraordinary architecture designed to resemble a 13th-century Italian Franciscan church, particularly the Basilica of Saint Francis of Assisi. Marble floors, gold ornamentation, stained glass, and soaring ceilings.

The Spanish religious-art workshop Talleres de Arte Granda, founded in Madrid in 1891, designed and furnished the church's interior.

It was founded by Mother Angelica, the founder of EWTN, and opened in 1999. Three donors provided all of the funds needed for construction and completion.

]]> Visulahti Wax Museum in Mikkeli, Finland Fri, 20 Nov 2026 12:00:00 -0500 https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/visulahti-wax-museum https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/visulahti-wax-museum

Rather than being an impressive, polished wax museum, the Visulahti Wax Museum has become famous for its awkward, outdated, and sometimes unintentionally hilarious figures.

The museum has something of a cult reputation in Finland. Its wax figures are famously questionable in quality: many look surprisingly inaccurate, while some remind you more of a horror movie setting. In 1983, the Wax Museum was established with serious intentions, but nowadays people visit it mainly for nostalgic reasons. You have to approach the museum with a good sense of humour. 

The collection rarely gets updated, and the once-popular TV stars are now unfamiliar to the younger audience. The newest figurine is the Finnish president, whose resemblance – or the lack of it – has been widely discussed in the national news.

There are also international stars displayed at the museum, such as Elvis, the Beatles, and Santa Claus. At the end of the tour, a creepy version of Mickey Mouse sings to you with his friends, as you walk out of the building, wondering what you just experienced. 

]]> wax museum City Island Nautical Museum in The Bronx, New York Fri, 20 Nov 2026 10:00:00 -0500 https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/city-island-nautical-museum https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/city-island-nautical-museum

It was perhaps inevitable that market-driven land use change would come to City Island; the beauty of the place is immediately apparent. Only a quarter-mile causeway separates the small island from the rest of the Bronx, one of the five boroughs of New York City, and yet City Island can seem a world away.

The former United Boat Service Yard at the foot of Carroll Street was the first major maritime property to be converted to residences, becoming in the early-1980s The Boatyard Condominiums. The managing director then of the island’s chamber of commerce told the New York Times, “If the condos do well, then the boatyards and marinas are all going to go.”

Less than 10 years later, the last sail-making loft, Rapsey & Lapthorn, founded in 1915 and a purveyor to America's Cup racing yachts, became The Sailmaker Condominium. All that was left of these two businesses was nominal references to their function before conversion to residential development. Yet, in spite of the loss of major historic waterfront industries, City Island (mostly, see “Know Before You Go”) maintains its small-town, maritime feel.

A half-mile wide and 1.5 miles long, one is never far from the water on City Island. The buildings, even the new construction, are low-rise, providing a sense of sky that is unique to waterfront communities. With only 4,417 residents (2020 Census) and a—“a” as in one—small supermarket, gas station, bank, and hardware store, it is not hard for visitors to picture themselves in a quaint New England fishing village.

The popular seafood restaurants, the principal tourist attraction, contribute to the impression. This is ironic because City Island was not a significant port for fishing vessels. City Island is known for its boat building and repair and if you want to know more about that history, the place to visit is the City Island Nautical Museum.

The museum is located in the former Public School 102 (later, P.S. 17) designed by noted academic architect C.B.J. Snyder and constructed in 1897. The museum contains a main hall gallery primarily composed of two-dimensional material; the Walsh Library with books, ephemera, and other artifacts; the Nautical Room that focuses on the island’s maritime history; a Community Room, which celebrates life on City Island; and the School Room, with an emphasis on local education.

Like many museums in sparsely populated places that have undergone substantial change, the historical museum on City Island is nostalgic, a lovingly handcrafted assemblage of what artifacts became available for exhibition and what might be reproduced (including with a photocopying machine). A larger physical space, and a much larger budget, might have resulted in a more polished presentation, but a good deal of the charm of the museum derives from the manner in which it tells the maritime and social history of City Island.

]]> ships maritime history museums Promotions Gallery in Paris, France Thu, 19 Nov 2026 16:00:00 -0500 https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/promotions-gallery https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/promotions-gallery

Historically, a secret entrance at the School of Mines, known as the “Mines staircase,” provided students access to the Paris Catacombs.

Although this private access is no longer available for use due to safety reasons, the General Inspector of Quarries still grants students permission to uphold this artistic tradition.

Each year, on the occasion of Sainte-Barbe, celebrated on December 4th in honor of the patron saint of miners, first-year students create a painting representing their class, continuing the tradition.

]]> mining paintings art Čigoč Stork Village in Kratečko, Croatia Thu, 19 Nov 2026 14:00:00 -0500 https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/cigoc-stork-village https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/cigoc-stork-village

In the Croatian village of Čigoč, some of the most conspicuous residents live above the rooftops. White storks build bulky nests on traditional wooden houses, sharing the settlement with the people below.

Situated in Lonjsko Polje Nature Park beside the Tišina oxbow of the Sava River, the village is surrounded by wet meadows, pastures, and pools. These habitats provide feeding grounds close to the nests, allowing adult birds to gather frogs, insects, and other small animals for their young.

In 1994, the conservation foundation EuroNatur named Čigoč the first European Stork Village. The designation recognised the village’s importance for white storks and its long-standing relationship between people, traditional farming, and wildlife. It also launched an initiative that would connect stork villages across Europe.

The wooden houses are part of this story. Their rooftops provide nesting places, while the surrounding agricultural landscape helps sustain the birds. During the breeding season, a walk through the village offers a chance to watch adults tending their nests and travelling between the rooftops and nearby feeding grounds.

]]> wildlife wildlife sanctuaries birds Thunder Hole in Bar Harbor, Maine Thu, 19 Nov 2026 12:00:00 -0500 https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/thunder-hole-in-acadia-national-park https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/thunder-hole-in-acadia-national-park

Located in Maine's Acadia National Park, along the rocky shoreline of Mount Desert Island, Thunder Hole is a natural geological formation known for producing a  booming, thunder-like sound phenomenon that gives it its name, as well as for explosive water sprays reaching up to 40 feet.

Resulting from glacial activity over thousands of years ago, what began as a small, natural fissure in the solid granite cliffs, slowly gave way to the 10 foot wide channel seen today. As high tide rolls in, and wave force increases, water rushes into this channel, and into a small underwater cavern contained therein.

When an incoming wave forces water into this cavern, trapped air in the cavern is compressed and then escapes, almost as if through the blow hole of a whale, with magnificent water sprays and reverberating claps that sound like thunder. 

Stand in awe on this rocky outcropping, as you take in the sweeping coastal views and the natural wonders that Mother Nature has provided. 

Thunder Hole is best viewed approx 2 hours before high tide (check google for tide tables).  

]]> geological oddities oceans water Abdulla Avloni Memorial Museum in Tashkent, Uzbekistan Thu, 19 Nov 2026 10:00:00 -0500 https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/abdulla-avloni-memorial-museum https://www.atlasobscura.com/places/abdulla-avloni-memorial-museum

Most memorial museums stay put in the house of the person they remember. This one moved out.

It was founded in 1968 in the Tashkent house where Abdulla Avloni (1878–1934) had lived with his family from 1910 until his death. Avloni was one of the Jadids, the Muslim reformers who believed Central Asia could be renewed through new-method schools, newspapers and the theatre. He opened schools, wrote their textbooks, published the newspaper Shuhrat and, in 1913, gathered the Turon theatre troupe.

In 1993 the museum left the house for the institute that carries Avloni's name, where teachers from all over Uzbekistan now come to brush up their skills. Without its original walls, it relies on things to bring him close: his desk, typewriter and candlestick, his bookcase and wardrobe, even his clothes, arranged in a reconstruction of his study.

Around them are early twentieth-century books and newspapers in Arabic script, printed in Tashkent, Kazan, Orenburg, Baku and Istanbul, and a small stage that recalls the Turon troupe. The most surprising corner is a tall red display in the middle of the hall, where Avloni and fellow reformers such as Mahmudkhoja Behbudi, brought to life with artificial intelligence, look out at visitors and present passages from their writings. Walk around to the back and there is a mirror with the words "Zamonamiz jadidi", "a Jadid of our time". Whoever looks into it becomes, for a moment, the newest member of the movement.

The museum is also the only one from Uzbekistan in the UMAC Worldwide Database of University Museums and Collections.

]]> education islam museums Podcast: Exploring Alberta’s Rich History in Fiction The Podcast Team Thu, 19 Nov 2026 07:15:00 -0500 https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/podcast-exploring-alberta-s-rich-history-in-fiction https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/podcast-exploring-alberta-s-rich-history-in-fiction

Listen and subscribe on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and all major podcast apps.

In this episode of The Atlas Obscura Podcast, we’re exploring the surprising side of Alberta with the Canadian novelist Esi Edugyan.

Our podcast is an audio guide to the world’s wondrous, awe-inspiring, strange places. In under 15 minutes, we’ll take you to an incredible site, and along the way you’ll meet some fascinating people and hear their stories. Join us daily, Monday through Thursday, to explore a new wonder with host Kelly McEvers and guests.

This is an edited transcript of the Atlas Obscura Podcast: a celebration of the world’s strange, incredible, and wondrous places. Find the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and all major podcast apps.

Esi Edugyan: I remember coming across this image of these Black homesteaders in Central and Northern Alberta kind of working the land. I hadn't had a sense of there being any Black presence or Black history in Alberta, and I thought, "Oh my gosh, who are these people?"

Kelly McEvers: I'm Kelly McEvers, and this is Atlas Obscura, a celebration of the world's strange, incredible, and wondrous places. This episode was produced in partnership with Travel Alberta: Explore Canada's Wild Side. This month we are talking to writers and artists who find inspiration in their home province of Alberta.

And today we're talking to novelist Esi Edugyan. She grew up in Calgary, Alberta, and her novels are part literary fiction, part adventure, traveling across continents and through different time periods. They're also based on her extensive historical research. She says she's inspired by what she calls the footnotes of history, these moments and stories that most of us have never heard of, in particular stories and histories of Black communities.

Unlike most surviving Cham towers that crown dramatic hilltops, Binh Lam Tower rises almost unexpectedly from the flat, verdant plains of a quiet lowland village.

Constructed around the late tenth to early eleventh century, this 20-meter brick sanctuary serves as a vital architectural bridge, catching the art form mid-evolution between the delicate, lyrical features of the My Son A1 style and the grand, spear-like forms of classic Binh Dinh towers.

Its weathered facade features slender vertical pilasters, mini-temple false doors, and faint relief carvings of the mythical bird-god Garuda. Beyond its standing brickwork, Binh Lam hides deep subterranean secrets: archaeological digs uncovered vast foundations of a once-extensive religious complex, alongside stone Nagas and relief sculptures.

Furthermore, the tower once formed the eastern heart of ancient Thi Nai Citadel, positioned along river channels leading to the historical port—making this lowland monument a crucial physical anchor to Champa's lost naval and architectural empire.

The National Underground Railroad Freedom Center, located in Cincinnati along the banks of the Ohio River makes a solemn statement about the lives that were lived enslaved in the early history of the United States, and the many heroic men and women who played important roles in the Underground Railroad movement, which helped to bring an end to African slavery in the United States.  Referred to as a "museum of conscience", The Freedom Center is dedicated to exploring the struggle to abolish human enslavement. During the era when the Underground Railroad was active, Cincinnati was a major gateway across the Ohio River where freedom seekers escaped from southern slave states to the northern states or Canada, making the Center's location rather significant. 

Having opened its doors in 2004, the Freedom Center uses immersive exhibits across multiple floors to convey an account that is simultaneously rich in the cultural traditions of the enslaved, as well as steeped in the violence and tragedies that were endured.  The histories are told through a combination of permanent and traveling exhibits that utilize storytelling, film, artwork, hands-on activities and more.  

Perhaps one of the most impressive and prominent displays at the center is an authentic, 19th-century reconstructed slave pen that was obtained from a farm in Kentucky. It stands as America's only remaining, pristinely preserved slave pen and stands as a stark reminder of the atrocious conditions that were endured.

The pen, originally built somewhere around 1830 by a wealthy Kentucky farmer, runaway slave catcher, and slave trader, was used as a holding facility for captured and purchased enslaved men, women and children. It was discovered, quite by accident in 1998 when a farmer, who was preparing to demolish an old barn on his property, discovered that the barn had been built up around this old pen, thus protecting and preserving (and hiding) the slave pen for more than 100 years.

During its unfortunate years of use, enslaved people would be kept in the pen, often for months, until the slave trader accumulated a large enough "stock" to march them further south to be sold. These forced marches would often cover upwards of 750 miles. Conditions in these pens would be brutal, offering no sanitation, lighting or warmth.  As many as 65 enslaved people would often be housed in this small pen.  Also very moving is the memorial room dedicated to the Transatlantic Slave Trade, as well as the Freedom's Eternal Flame Terrace which overlooks the Ohio River and the city skyline. 

The National Underground Railroad Freedom Center is a beautiful and meaningful tribute to the human right for freedom, and to the brave men, women and children who stood up to the inhuman treatment of themselves and of others; and to those who continue to fight for the cause of freedom through out the world today.

Above the village of Kalnik in northern Croatia, the walls of Veliki Kalnik Castle rise from a jagged rocky ridge. Built across several levels, the medieval stronghold follows the natural contours of the rock, making its surviving towers and walls appear to grow out of the mountain.

First documented in 1243, the castle is best known for a story involving King Béla IV of Hungary and Croatia. According to local legend, the king took refuge here during the Mongol invasion of the 13th century. As the siege dragged on and supplies dwindled, villagers kept the defenders fed with plums.

The grateful king is said to have rewarded his rescuers with noble status. They became known as the kalnički šljivari—the “plum nobles of Kalnik.” This tale remains part of the region’s identity, connecting an imposing fortress with an unexpectedly humble fruit.

The ruins visible today developed over centuries. Their towers, fragments of walls, and elevated viewpoints reveal how the builders used the steep terrain as part of the castle’s defenses. From the heights, the view opens across the villages, fields, and wooded hills below.

In the highland villages of North Toraja, the skyline is dominated by tongkonan—traditional ancestral houses with sweeping, boat-shaped saddle roofs that loom dramatically over the landscape. For centuries, these wooden structures have served as the spiritual and social anchor for Torajan clans, decorated strictly according to Aluk Todolo ("the way of the ancestors"), the indigenous animist belief system. Their facades are traditionally adorned with carved geometric patterns (pa'ssura'), water buffalo horns (kabongo'), and sculpted wooden heads (katik) symbolizing wealth, status, and protection.

However, in the small hamlet of Tolu Deri, just north of Rantepao, one particular tongkonan stands out as a striking, visually arresting symbol of modern Torajan syncretism. Mounted directly onto the front gabled peak of the structure—occupying the exact position traditionally reserved for ancestral motifs—is a massive wooden crucifix bearing a carved figure of Jesus Christ.

While the majority of the Torajan population converted to Christianity (predominantly Dutch Reformed Protestantism and Catholicism) during the 20th century, the integration of Christian motifs into traditional architecture usually remains subtle, such as small carved crosses on support beams or church roofs built in the tongkonan shape. Seeing a full-scale, dramatic crucifix physically fused into the facade of a traditional house—standing directly above the customary buffalo head and skull mountings—is exceptionally rare.

This unique blending of iconographies visually captures the lived reality of Toraja today: a culture where deeply rooted Christian faith does not replace ancestral traditions, but rather sits alongside them in a harmonious, visually striking synthesis.
