documents.text: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost Hugging Face Search models, datasets, users... Ctrl K Models Datasets Spaces Buckets Docs Enterprise Pricing Website Tasks HuggingChat Collections Languages Organizations Community Blog Posts Daily Papers Hardware Learn Discord Forum GitHub Solutions Team & Enterprise Hugging Face PRO Enterprise Support Inference Providers Inference Endpoints Storage Buckets Log In Sign Up Back to Articles Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost Published November 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 29 +23 Younes B ybelkada Follow ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Nathan Habib SaylorTwift Follow Lysandre lysandre Follow Amine Dirhoussi aminediroHF Follow Adithya S K AdithyaSK Follow shaun smith evalstate Follow Sergio Paniego sergiopaniego Follow Joel Niklaus joelniklaus Follow Lewis Tunstall lewtun Follow TL;DR Table of Contents Training inside agent harnesses Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face Three sources Validation with openenv validate Difficulty check with the base model Testing the filters with short training runs The dataset AsyncGRPOTrainer for more efficient GRPO training Training setup Training infrastructure Final mixture safeagents in the loop Super-adapter: merging all adapters into one Adapter merging evaluation results Final results Training results Evaluation results Open question: What did the model really learn to do? Closing words and future directions Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution. Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination. Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time. Our earlier work ( multi-harness RL , harness adapters ) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations. TL;DR We trained one LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B per agent harness (pi, Hermes Agent, OpenCode), with RL inside the harness itself. Datasets, training and agent rollouts all happen on the Hub in Jobs using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer , OpenEnv and harbor. Each harness adapter beats the base model under its own harness on both benchmarks, for both performance and efficiency. The three LoRAs are also merged into a single super adapter that runs unchanged under pi, Hermes Agent and OpenCode. All artifacts (adapters, GGUFs, RL tasks, safeagents plugin) can be browsed through this Hugging Face collection . Table of Contents Training inside agent harnesses Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face Testing the filters with short training runs AsyncGRPOTrainer for more efficient GRPO training Training setup Super-adapter: merging all adapters into one Final results Open question: What did the model really learn to do? Closing words and future directions Training inside agent harnesses We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2 , OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6 . The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol: Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop , SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM 's agent and environment classes, slime 's custom rollout functions, or ART 's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer. Generating custom RL tasks on Hugging Face For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv . We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains. RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything. This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate , and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B. Three sources Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves: SWE-smith ( Python , Go ) injects bugs into real Python and Go repositories, with an LLM rewrite or a mutation such as a flipped operator. The tests that catch each bug become the task's tests. It adds volume. SWE-Gym, packaged as Harbor tasks in TaskTrove , turns real GitHub issues and their merged fixes into tasks. It adds real-world bugs. Tasksmith generates tasks from merged pull requests. An LLM agent writes the instruction and tests, and Tasksmith checks the result: the reference and a valid alternative must pass, while the unfixed code and a known-wrong solution must fail. We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest. Validation with openenv validate A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials: The reference solution earns the maximum reward ( semantic.oracle_max ). Doing nothing scores clearly lower ( semantic.floor_gap ). No canary scores more than doing nothing ( semantic.canary_floor ). A replay of the reference gives the same reward ( runtime.episode_determinism ). Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task: openenv validate path/to/task --sandbox hf-sandbox 858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded. Difficulty check with the base model A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository. Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks. Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all. This example shows how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation. Testing the filters with short training runs The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1. Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer , on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered: Unvalidated : 24 accepted tasks plus 8 that failed validation. Validated : 32 accepted tasks, chosen without regard to difficulty. Unqualified : 32 accepted tasks that the base model always or never solves. Qualified : 32 accepted tasks that the base model solves on some attempts. The figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status. The dataset harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config. Source Task type Tasks Qualified SWE-smith Injected bugs in Python and Go 717 144 SWE-Gym (TaskTrove) Real GitHub issues 130 27 Tasksmith Generated from merged pull requests 24 22 Total 871 171 AsyncGRPOTrainer for more efficient GRPO training We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step. For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost . Training setup To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer . The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison. The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which showed that 0.1 worked best). We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs. Training infrastructure Each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes). As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step. Final mixture The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade . In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below: Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture. safeagents in the loop We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup. The number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter. Super-adapter: merging all adapters into one Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness? We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere. We concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat" ). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging ( task arithmetic , TIES , KnOTS ) finds that scaling each update below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters: ⅓ (the average): each harness keeps only a third of its own update. ½: each update at half strength. 1 (the plain sum): every update applied in full. Weight pi hermes opencode All three harnesses Tool calls per task base model 39.1% 46.0% 44.8% 43.3% 49.2 ⅓ (average) 49.4% 51.2% 47.1% 49.2% 35.6 ½ 48.8% 53.5% 55.2% 52.5% 25.9 1 (sum) 40.2% 62.8% 47.1% 50.0% 13.4 The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own update. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½. Adapter merging evaluation results Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model): Harness Benchmark Qwen3.8-27B Qwen3.8-27B-<harness>-adapted Qwen3.8-27B-super-adapter Qwen3.8-27B , thinking Qwen3.8-27B-super-adapter , thinking pi SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 40.0% 64.0% (−60%) 46.0% (−73%) 74.0% 74.0% (−48%) hermes SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 29.4% 43.1% (−56%) 47.1% (−60%) 45.1% 60.8% (−36%) opencode SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 35.3% 51.0% (−72%) 45.1% (−63%) 47.1% 66.7% (−31%) pi Terminal-Bench 2.1 40.0% 56.5% (−56%) 48.2% (−56%) 52.9% 57.6% (−25%) hermes Terminal-Bench 2.1 44.7% 58.8% (−70%) 55.3% (−53%) 58.8% 63.5% (−19%) opencode Terminal-Bench 2.1 47.6% 52.4% (−53%) 52.4% (−68%) 54.9% 58.5% (−22%) "Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off. With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001). Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties. Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist. The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same. The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card . Final results This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses. Training results Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens. During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below. On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked. Evaluation results This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check. Evaluation setup We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi does not keep previous reasoning turns while OpenCode and Hermes do, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions. Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval. For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks. For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories . Final evaluation results All three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035). The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section ). Each model card has the full paired results. Does the efficiency and performance ability transfer across harnesses? To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode. Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses. Evaluation on out-of-distribution tasks and setup What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with? We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with? Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it. Model pass@1 (all assertions met) vs base Partial credit (share of assertions met) vs base base 23.0% 62.2% pi 160 27.0% +4.0 66.2% +4.0 opencode 150 25.3% +2.3 65.2% +3.0 merged 23.7% +0.7 60.6% −1.6 hermes 160 17.7% −5.3 56.6% −5.6 Open question: What did the model really learn to do? We appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5 . This question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand. This phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well. Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community. However this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results. Closing words and future directions Throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters . In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models. We also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future. Google Research Google AI Learn about all our AI Google DeepMind Explore the frontier of AI Google Labs Try our AI experiments Research Resources Conferences & events Careers Blog About Search Home Blog How Google Duplex evolved to also call businesses for you in Gemini November 20, 2026 Yossi Matias, Vice President, Google & GM, Google Research, Yaniv Leviathan, Google Fellow, Google Research, and Janet Zhou, Group Product Manager, Google Maps When we introduced Google Duplex in 2018, it pioneered natural voice conversations between AI and local businesses over the phone. Since then, this technology has worked behind the scenes across many Google products. These capabilities are integrated directly in Tasks in Gemini . Quick links Tasks in Gemini Share Copy link × Completing tasks like making dinner reservations or booking a hair appointment is time consuming. Live phone conversations move fast and rarely follow a script. The person on the other end can say almost anything, often revising their thoughts mid-sentence – and people often rely on subtle tone changes to indicate whose turn it is to speak. Pause half a second too long, and it sounds like the call dropped; speak too soon, and you end up talking over each other. Leveraging AI to complete these tasks respectfully over the phone required us to consider high quality speech understanding, contextual reasoning, and speech synthesis working together in a single, low-latency system. We introduced Google Duplex nearly a decade ago to help address this challenge. Propelled by advances in foundation models, the Duplex architecture has evolved to power autonomous task completion across many core products, such as Google Search and Maps. This week, we launched Duplex in Tasks in Gemini App , a personal AI collaborator that can help coordinate real-world chores, like calling businesses for you and handling real-world requests on behalf of the user. In this post, we look back at the decade-long architectural evolution that made this possible — moving from early, closed-domain models to a unified stack built entirely with Gemini. From closed-domain calls to Tasks in Gemini What began as a narrow, task-specific system quickly expanded into a shared conversational infrastructure, built in collaboration with teams across Google. During the COVID-19 pandemic, when business hours and services shifted rapidly, Duplex doubled down on verifying merchant info automatically to keep listings accurate. It remains an important data source; for example, business information sourced from Duplex’s phone calls had been shown in Search and Maps over one trillion times , as we shared in 2023. Simultaneously, we worked with Android and hardware teams to bring these conversational models directly on-device. Starting in 2019, we rolled out new Pixel Call Assist features across five consecutive Pixel generations. These models continue to power features like Call Screen and Hold for Me , helping users filter unknown callers and speak with a live agent when a hold queue ends until the user rejoins. In 2025 and 2026, foundation models unlocked broader agentic calling in Google Search and Ask Maps , checking quotes, product availability, and service openings from pet grooming to auto repair. Three generations of conversational architecture Over the past decade, the stack behind these calls evolved through three distinct eras, moving from bespoke neural pipelines to a unified architecture using Gemini. 1. Pre-LLM closed-domain models We started work on Google Duplex before modern language models and even before the transformer itself was invented. In these early days, to ensure businesses and users had a great experience, we constrained Duplex to narrow domains and trained custom recurrent neural network models on anonymized, task-specific phone conversations. Without pre-trained world knowledge, we taught our models how to handle every specific type of task efficiently. In practice, this meant relying on extensive training data for each task type — such as interpreting the rigid flow of restaurant booking versus checking holiday hours — to ensure the system could reliably navigate domain-specific logic. 2. Early generative models and hybrid stacks Google Duplex started employing open domain foundation models in production as they emerged. For example, in 2022 Duplex used LaMDA in live calls. These pre-trained models simplified comprehension and common-sense reasoning, allowing the system to handle unexpected conversational turns and tangents, while remaining grounded in the context like a standard restaurant booking. However, these early generative models were less predictable and sometimes slower than today's, so we built hybrid stacks that paired generative models for flexible phrasing with deterministic state tracking and strict policy guardrails. This helped ensure that both users and businesses had a great experience. 3. Unbounded tasks and Gemini integration As foundation models advanced, we removed the constraint of fixed verticals entirely by shifting to prompting the system with free-text task descriptions. This allowed models to define a task simply via a prompt, enabling the system to generalize to new task types and nuances (like asking for window seating or extra space for a stroller) and new business categories, without building separate dialogue models from scratch. Our calling stack uses Gemini to unify multimodal understanding, planning, and dialogue generation so the system can navigate multi-constraint requests — like scheduling car maintenance around calendar conflicts — and adapt when a receptionist suggests another slot. Technical hurdles in live telephony Even with frontier models, live telephony poses hurdles that pre-training on standard datasets like the web alone doesn't solve: Pragmatic grounding for pre-call and conversational context, and real-world intent understanding: The web doesn’t have all the data needed to capture how calls unfold with busy merchants. Nearly a decade of experience with goal-directed calls helps our stack grasp pragmatic norms, starting even before the call. In practice, this means matching a free-text task with a business based on the historical context of past conversations (e.g., knowing a specific vendor doesn't take reservations for large groups over the weekend) to predict whether a task will work. During the call, this helps the model determine what makes sense to ask at a given moment, how to read polite indirect refusals, and how to keep calls brief and effective. Sub-second latency in noisy acoustic setups: Calls run over compressed phone lines against loud backdrops like clattering in kitchens, espresso machines, street noise, and side chatter. Our stack is tuned for low-latency streaming inference so replies land at a natural cadence. Custom acoustic and conversation cadence models assist the core AI system with handling background noise and pauses, stop talking when expected, etc. Designing for both ends of the line Duplex has to work just as well for the business answering the phone as it does for the user. That principle shaped several design choices: Clear disclosure. Every call opens by clearly disclosing that it’s an AI agent — specifically, an automated system calling from Google. Businesses stay in control. Merchants can opt out of automated calls in their Google Business Profile settings, or simply say “Please stop calling my business” during a call. No setup and zero adaptation. Duplex works through the phone a business already answers: no software to install, no booking system to maintain and no staff to train. Whoever answers can handle the call the way they would with any customer, even mid-rush with a line at the counter. One conversation, many insights. Details gathered on one call can answer many later questions, so a business isn’t asked the same thing over and over. For example, Google Maps can show details that Duplex gathers about businesses, like happy hour specials, patio seating, pet-friendliness, a parking tip or even a weekly trivia night. Conclusion Many daily errands, local services, and urgent tasks still require speaking directly with another person to coordinate details reliably. By integrating Duplex’s capabilities into Tasks in Gemini App, we are taking another step toward closing this loop. Natural voice interaction becomes a seamlessly integrated modality that the agent can deploy whenever structured digital channels like online APIs or booking forms don't exist. Using our newest Gemini 4 models — including Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Neon — Tasks in Gemini can now support more comprehensive workflows like analyzing utility bills, processing transactions securely via the Agent Payments Protocol , and coordinating with users over email and Rich Communication Services (RCS). Through these capabilities, we are bringing this research into the next generation of AI assistance. Acknowledgements We’re thankful to the Duplex team and to everyone across Google leading and involved in this decade-long journey.For driving the transition to Gemini-powered calling and making this launch in Tasks in Gemini possible, we're especially grateful to Yoav Tzur, Sasha Goldshtein, Rafael Goldfarb, Liran Peretz, Ritika Pathak, Sen Li, Ran Manor, Dekel Auster, and many others across the team. This publication is available at https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ukeu-summit-2026-key-documents/uk-eu-summit-2026-joint-statement-html We, the Leaders of the European Union (EU) and of the United Kingdom (UK), held our second EU-UK Summit in Brussels on 20 November 2026. Against the backdrop of deepening geopolitical and economic challenges, we reaffirm our support for an ambitious and dynamic relationship that delivers for our citizens and concluded the following: 1. The EU and the UK are neighbours, friends, and like-minded, strategically important partners, facing shared threats and aligned on defending the rules-based international order rooted in the principles of the United Nations Charter. Our partnership reflects the strength of our common values: democracy, the rule of law, and respect for human rights. In the increasingly complex and challenging geopolitical context, we are committed to working closely together within our Strategic Partnership and to fulfil our shared responsibility for the security of Europe and beyond. 2. The first EU-UK Summit of 19 May 2025 marked a significant positive development in our bilateral relations with our new Strategic Partnership. We agreed that this would build on the stable foundation for our relationship set by the Withdrawal Agreement, including the Windsor Framework, and the Trade and Cooperation Agreement and reaffirmed our commitment to their full, timely and faithful implementation. Having jointly reviewed the implementation of the Trade and Cooperation Agreement as required by Article 776 of the Agreement, we affirm that the agreement functions effectively, notwithstanding certain barriers which require that we deploy further efforts to address them. 3. We continue to deliver on the Common Understanding agreed between the European Commission and the UK government on “A renewed agenda for European Union-United Kingdom cooperation”. Building on our shared commitment for a strong partnership, the EU and the UK have agreed on a series of deliverables to further deepen our cooperation. 4. We are implementing the EU-UK Security and Defence Partnership, strengthening our strategic partnership across the foreign policy, peace, security and defence spectrum. 5. We reaffirm our commitment to the full, timely and faithful implementation of the Withdrawal Agreement, welcome progress made and commit to accelerate the work ahead. We will ensure that all citizens are able to fully enjoy their rights, now and in the future. We will protect the Windsor Framework’s vital role in avoiding a hard border on the island of Ireland, bringing benefits to Northern Ireland and protecting the integrity of the UK internal market, while accelerating the delivery of the safeguards for the protection of the EU Single Market in all areas. We will finalise the work to implement the Protocol relating to the Sovereign Base Areas in Cyprus in all its parts. 6. We welcome the signature and provisional application of the EU-UK Agreement in respect of Gibraltar as well as the benefits it brings to the whole region and look forward to its conclusion. COMMON GLOBAL PRIORITIES 7. We reaffirm our unwavering support for Ukraine’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders, and condemn Russia’s unprovoked and unjustified war of aggression as a manifest violation of international law including the UN Charter. We reiterate our call on Russia to immediately end its war of aggression against Ukraine and agree to a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire. The path to peace in Ukraine cannot be decided without Ukraine. We will continue working in close partnership throughout the negotiating process, with the shared objective of achieving a comprehensive and lasting peace. 8. The military and civilian support to Ukraine by the UK and the EU has been crucial so far in supporting Ukraine in its defence against Russia’s war of aggression. We will continue to provide, in coordination with like-minded partners and allies, political, economic, financial, military, humanitarian and diplomatic support to Ukraine for as long as it takes and call on international partners to swiftly step up their support to help meet Ukraine’s pressing financing and military needs. We will continue to strengthen our coordination to increase pressure on Russia, notably via sanctions, countering its hybrid activities and working towards achieving a comprehensive, just and lasting peace, based on the principles of the UN Charter and international law and underpinned by robust and credible security guarantees for Ukraine. We will continue cooperation on Ukraine’s recovery and reconstruction, including through the Ukraine Facility. 9. We are engaging on the wider Eastern European neighbourhood, including the Black Sea. We also remain committed to support the Republic of Moldova in its efforts to address Russia’s persistent and evolving hybrid attacks and challenges stemming from Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. 10. We reaffirm our commitment to the stability and prosperity of the Western Balkans. We agreed to work together on strengthening their internal reform agendas, including the rule of law, democracy, fight against corruption and organised crime, addressing shared security challenges and promoting sustainable economic growth. 11. We reiterate our call for respect for international law, international humanitarian law and protection of civilians, unimpeded access and sustained distribution of humanitarian assistance at scale into and throughout Gaza, and condemn settler violence and settlement expansion in the West Bank. The EU and the UK call on Israel to withdraw its tender for construction in the E1 area. We reiterate our commitment to UNSCR 2803 to deliver peace and stability in Gaza. We are clear that Hamas must permanently decommission its weapons and have no role in the future governance of Gaza. We welcome the Team Gaza initiative and call for international coordination in humanitarian assistance and recovery and reconstruction efforts. We reiterate our support for the Palestinian Authority. We support a comprehensive, just and lasting peace based on the two-state solution, in accordance with relevant UN Security Council Resolutions and the New York Declaration, where two democratic states, Israel and Palestine, live side-by side in peace within secure and recognised borders. 12. We reiterate our full support for Lebanon’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. We call for the full implementation of UNSCR 1701, support the strengthening of the Lebanese Armed Forces and implementation of the US-Israel-Lebanon Trilateral Framework agreed in June. We reaffirm the importance of continued international support in Lebanon including following the end of UNIFIL’s mandate. 13. We condemn Iran’s attacks against countries in the region and on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and stand in solidarity with our regional partners. We firmly support diplomatic efforts to avoid further conflict in the region and ensure the restoration of freedom of navigation and transit passage, as enshrined in UNCLOS. We reaffirmed our commitment to a lasting diplomatic resolution to address both the Strait of Hormuz and Iran’s nuclear issue. Iran must never acquire a nuclear weapon and must cooperate fully with the IAEA. Iran must stop its destabilising activities in the region and its hybrid attacks on European soil. 14. We condemn the Houthi military escalation in Yemen and against Saudi Arabia and call upon the Houthis to immediately cease all military action, including all attacks against civilian shipping which threaten maritime security in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait. We call upon the Houthis to allow humanitarian access to alleviate the suffering of the civilian population. 15. Alongside African partners, we will further deepen cooperation on peace, stability and prosperity in Africa. We reaffirm our shared interest in a secure and prosperous Indo-Pacific and we will strengthen our engagement on and with the region. We will also explore closer cooperation in the Arctic. 16. Cooperation on security and defence is a shared priority, in particular in the face of the long-term threat posed by Russia to our security. This includes working towards building a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO. In the current security environment, for the EU, the mutually reinforcing strategic partnership with NATO is essential for Euro-Atlantic security. For the UK and 23 EU Member States that are also NATO allies, the Atlantic Alliance remains the foundation of their collective defence. We will enhance coordination and strengthen European security, including through support for Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. 17. We reaffirm our commitment to effective multilateralism, with the United Nations at its core, respect for international law, and our unwavering support for the international criminal justice system, particularly the International Criminal Court, which is a fundamental part of the rules-based international order. We deeply regret attacks or threats against the Court, its elected officials, its personnel and those cooperating with the Court. Together we will continue to support the impartiality and integrity of the ICC and we stand ready to take all the necessary measures to ensure that the Court continues to operate effectively and fulfils its indispensable mandate. 18. We reaffirm our mutual commitment to a free, sustainable, fair and open rules-based international trade system with the World Trade Organization at its core. We will actively support the WTO reform process in Geneva and step up our cooperation, bilaterally and in dedicated new formats with like-minded partners, including through EU and Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) cooperation, to promote deep and comprehensive reform, while preserving predictability and rules-based international trade. We also support the work done by the OECD which plays an essential role for international economic cooperation. 19. As the United Kingdom assumes the G20 Presidency in 2027, we reaffirm our commitment to the G20’s core mission of international economic cooperation. We will continue to strengthen coordination of macroeconomic policies, safeguard global financial stability and promote strong, sustainable and inclusive growth. Recognising the transformative potential of artificial intelligence for the global economy, we will seek to harness its benefits for growth and prosperity, while promoting its safe and responsible development and use. 20. We agree to pursue and wherever necessary to strengthen EU–UK cooperation on the international dimensions of climate security and to pursue close exchanges, as appropriate, in support of ambitious implementation of the Paris Agreement and the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, as well as in relevant multilateral negotiations on climate and environmental issues, including on plastics and the ocean. We remain committed to working with partners, for our shared security and prosperity, in accelerating the necessary global energy transition. BILATERAL PRIORITIES AND ACTIONS I. Peace, security and defence, development and health security 21. In an increasingly unstable and volatile world, the EU and UK restate our shared responsibility for the security of Europe. The global context makes strengthening our strategic partnership across the foreign policy, peace, security and defence spectrum a priority. We agree on the need to strengthen our cooperation on security and defence, commensurate with the threats Europe faces and the contribution the EU and the UK can make together, building on the EU-UK security and Defence Partnership and the progress made since its adoption. 22. The EU and the UK agree to stand together, enhancing our strategic partnership on foreign policy, peace, security and defence. We have today committed to a new shared ambition across the range of peace, security and defence cooperation, in recognition of the exceptional breadth and depth of our partnership. We will strengthen our support for Ukraine, and agree closer coordination on countering hybrid threats, maritime security and freedom of navigation, crisis management and defence industrial cooperation, where appropriate, and capability development. We will consult more regularly and connect respective capabilities more effectively and we will coordinate rapidly in response to serious security challenges, translating our partnership into practical cooperation and coordinated action. Given the global security context, we intend to enhance exchanges on defence industrial issues and will identify ways to deepen capability collaboration, taking into account the objective of developing resilient European supply chains and capabilities and addressing critical capability gaps, including through the Capability Coalitions. 23. Since the last Summit and the adoption of the EU-UK Security and Defence Partnership, we have held our High Level Foreign and Security Policy and Security and Defence Dialogues. We will continue regular strategic consultations on Russia/Ukraine, Western Balkans, and hybrid threats. We will further enhance EU-UK dialogue and cooperation on other thematic and geographic areas of joint interest, including holding our first Indo-Pacific strategic consultation and upgrading the existing consultations on Africa and the Middle East. We will also continue strengthening consultation and coordination on global challenges, including within the United Nations as well as in the G7 and G20 frameworks, and advance joint or mutually reinforcing initiatives in key regions and multilateral fora, together with partners from around the world. We will strengthen practical cooperation, including through reciprocal secondments and increased joint training. 24. Ukraine’s security is Europe’s security. Cooperation in support of Ukraine’s security will remain a priority. The EU Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine (EUMAM Ukraine) and the UK will continue to support the training of Ukrainian Armed Forces and to coordinate closely with the Coalition of the Willing, co-led by the UK, France and Germany, including in the context of the Multinational Force Ukraine. 25. We welcome the UK’s participation under the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan as a major step forward in our support for Ukraine. 26. All of the above is without prejudice to the specific character of the security and defence policy of certain EU Member States, and taking into account the security and defence interests of all Member States, in accordance with the EU Treaties. 27. The EU and the UK will continue to closely cooperate in crisis management and step up cooperation in the context of civilian missions under the Common Security and Defence Policy. In this context we welcome the conclusion of negotiations on the Framework Participation Agreement for UK participation in EU civilian CSDP missions, enabling a tangible joint contribution to tackle shared threats and challenges, with a particular focus on European security. 28. Recognising that security also depends on the effective deployment of materiel, equipment and personnel, the EU and UK agree that cooperation on military mobility, including logistics, is vitally important. We welcome progress on advancing UK participation in the PESCO Military Mobility and Network of Logistic Hubs projects, and agree to deepen practical cooperation between the EU and UK to support the rapid movement of forces across Europe, ensuring that such cooperation remains fit for purpose and delivers greater efficiency in military mobility arrangements and noting the importance of EU-NATO cooperation in this field. 29. Reaffirming our support for the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and freedom of navigation, we have committed to deepening our engagement on maritime security, including through joint naval activities and enhanced cooperation on the challenges posed by the shadow fleet, countering their operations and activities. To this end, we will enhance information sharing and exchanges of best practices on tackling Russia’s shadow fleet, and coordinate efforts on enforcement actions and countering sanctions circumvention. We will strengthen practical cooperation on the protection and resilience of critical maritime infrastructure. We have committed to the “No Tolls/No Fees” pledge, championing multilateral cooperation, rejecting coercion and unilateral actions or measures that would hamper or impair lawful navigation. 30. To stand together against increasing hybrid and cyber threats intended to destabilise our societies, the EU and the UK have agreed on enhanced cooperation to strengthen our collective preparedness, resilience and response. We will enhance awareness of the threat landscape, improve our preparedness including through exercises, enhance cooperation to impose costs on hostile actors and coordinate responses, as well as to provide support to partners in their effort to increase resilience. We will also share best practice on our own civil and societal resilience, while continuing to cooperate closely in multilateral fora, including on promoting accountability and responsible state behaviour in cyberspace. We have strengthened cooperation on countering foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) both bilaterally and in multilateral fora, with a focus on information sharing and collective responses, and will continue to do so. 31. The UK and the EU will develop a dialogue to reinforce cooperation on democratic resilience, focusing on shared challenges, including strengthening the resilience of democratic institutions, safeguarding the integrity of the information space, supporting electoral integrity, as well as supporting relevant stakeholders, including civil society, to increase capacity to defend common democratic principles, and boosting citizens’ engagement and societal resilience. This will include the sharing of information and best practices in these areas. 32. We also intend to explore new avenues of cooperation on cybersecurity under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement to enhance our efforts to prevent, deter and respond to increasingly sophisticated threats. 33. EU and UK positions continue to align across multilateral fora and we will further step up our joint diplomatic outreach. Reinforcing our shared commitment to international law, human rights, democracy and free and fair elections worldwide, we welcome the signature of an Administrative Arrangement enabling UK participation in EU Election Observation Missions. 34. We are enhancing our cooperation on consular affairs, peace mediation and conflict prevention, climate and security, and addressing space threats. We continue engagement on counterterrorism and preventing violent extremism, disarmament, non-proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, as well as countering illicit trade in small arms and light weapons. We are intensively cooperating to ensure that our restrictive measures are aligned as much as possible. 35. We welcome the signature on 24 June 2026 of administrative arrangements in the area of development cooperation, and in international disaster and humanitarian response. These arrangements will contribute to strengthening our global resilience. 36. We look forward to the signature of the Memorandum of Understanding on health security, including matters concerning medical countermeasures, and look forward to finalising the establishment of the Specialised Committee on Health Security within the framework of the Trade and Cooperation Agreement. II. Putting people at the centre of the EU-UK relationship 37. We attach key importance to the objective in the Common Understanding of people-to-people ties being at the core of the renewed EU-UK agenda, particularly for the younger generation. 38. We underline the significance of the UK’s participation in Erasmus+ in 2027. The Erasmus+ funding call opened for applications on 18 November 2026. The UK and the EU encourage eligible institutions to apply to make the most of the opportunities offered by the Erasmus+ programme for benefitting learners of all ages, young people and staff across school education, vocational education and training, higher education, adult education, youth and sport. We agree to explore opportunities beyond 2027. 39. We welcome the conclusion of negotiations on a Youth Experience Scheme (YES). The scheme will allow 100 000 young people from the EU and the UK respectively to reside for up to three years to engage in activities such as work, studies, au-pairing, volunteering, or simply travelling, in accordance with our respective legal frameworks. We aim to apply this agreement no later than 2028 and endeavour to ensure that opportunities under the scheme will be available to our young people no later than January 2030. 40. Building on our joint commitments in the 2025 Common Understanding to deepen our people-to-people ties, particularly for the younger generation, and the UK’s association to the Erasmus+ programme in 2027, the UK and the EU share the objective of further increasing opportunities for studying, as well as other activities under Erasmus+ across the UK and the EU. The UK and the EU jointly recognise the importance of our shared strength in higher education to equip our young people with the skills they need to support economic growth and European competitiveness. 41. The EU and UK will therefore work towards a supplementing agreement to the Trade and Cooperation Agreement on tuition fees for EU students in the UK and for UK students in the EU. The Agreement will apply to all students from the other Party irrespective of the immigration pathway. The aim is to increase opportunities for students to study in each other’s territories. We will conclude the negotiations within six months from the date of the summit. 42. We welcome the ongoing successful implementation of the PeacePlus programme and will explore the development of the successor programme 2028-2034. We agree to explore opportunities to further expand contacts and exchanges for the strengthening of people-to-people ties in the EU and the UK beyond 2027. 43. The EU and the UK reaffirm the value of cultural and artistic exchanges, including the activities of touring artists. The EU and the UK should explore further mutually beneficial solutions. This year, the UK and the European Commission held the first High Level Meeting on Culture. The European Commission and the UK will continue to convene in this forum annually. III. Strengthening our economies while protecting our planet and its resources 44. We share the view that it is in our joint interest to strengthen our economic relations and generate prosperity, while protecting our planet and its resources. In this light, we recognise the importance of the full, timely and faithful implementation of the Common Understanding and of the Trade and Cooperation Agreement in bringing this agenda forward. 45. We note the decision of the Partnership Council 2/2025 of 19 June 2025 to continue our energy cooperation through an extension of the application of Part Two, Heading One, Title VIII (the Energy Title) of the Trade and Cooperation Agreement until 31 March 2027. We welcome the decision of the Partnership Council to further extend the application of the Energy Title until 31 March 2028. This is in line with our shared political understanding that the Energy Title should be pursued on a continuous basis. 46. We welcome the EU-UK Competition Cooperation Agreement as a supplementing agreement to the Trade and Cooperation Agreement. This is a step forward for enhanced competition cooperation and coordination. 47. We note the decision on full reciprocal access to waters to fish until 30 June 2038, which both parties will fully respect. In light of our international obligations, we reiterate our commitment to work together to ensure sustainability of the fisheries we share, by reinforcing our cooperation, continuing our practice of jointly agreed management measures of shared stocks, as appropriate, and improving the regional planning of measures impacting fishing activities. In particular, we will look at how to reverse the declines in key vulnerable species in the interest of protecting our shared fisheries and coastal communities. We agree on the need to work together collectively with other coastal States to rapidly conclude comprehensive sharing arrangements for stocks of common interest that are managed multilaterally to prevent detrimental effects for our fisheries sectors and coastal communities, as well as to address unsustainable and illegal fishing. 48. We welcome the conclusion of the negotiations on a Common Sanitary and Phytosanitary Area with certain common quality standards (SPS Agreement) which would allow that the vast majority of movements of animals, animal products, plants and plant products between Great Britain and the Crown Dependencies and the EU take place without the certificates or controls that are currently required. These same benefits would be extended to the movements between Great Britain and Northern Ireland, through the interplay of the SPS Agreement and the Windsor Framework, while maintaining Northern Ireland’s unique access to both the UK Internal Market and the EU Single Market. We aim to apply this agreement from 1 March 2028. 49. We welcome the conclusion of the negotiations on linking the EU and the UK Emissions Trading Systems (ETS agreement). This would provide a stable basis for allowing mutual recognition of EU and UK allowances and for exempting EU and UK goods from respective Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms subject to respective laws and procedures that we plan to launch without delays. We aim to apply this agreement from 2028. 50. The SPS and ETS agreements will strengthen bilateral trade, while ensuring a level playing field and sustainable development. We look forward to the conclusion of these agreements, together with the Youth Experience Scheme, in accordance with our respective legal frameworks, and their joint and timely entry into force. 51. We welcome our ongoing cooperation on security of energy supply, especially in critical times of geopolitical uncertainty. 52. We welcome the conclusion of exploratory talks in December 2025, and the progress made towards an agreement on the UK’s participation in the EU internal electricity market. Any such agreement would be linked to a UK financial contribution to reducing economic, social and territorial disparities between regions of the EU. The participation of the UK in the EU’s internal electricity market would contribute to enhanced energy security, decrease dependency on fossil fuels, improve the efficiency of electricity trading, facilitate cross border cooperation projects and provide more predictability for market participants and lower electricity costs. We commit to conclude these negotiations in 2027, subject to final agreement by both parties, in order for all the necessary arrangements to take effect as soon as possible. 53. We welcome the significant progress achieved in discussions on the mutual recognition of professional qualifications for architects as provided for in the Trade and Cooperation Agreement. We agree to expedite the conclusion of this process and explore opportunities for arrangements in other professions, including through working together to facilitate further expressions of interest. Within the framework provided by the Trade and Cooperation Agreement, we will also continue the discussions under the dedicated dialogue on the entry and temporary stay of natural persons for business purposes, including the sponsorship scheme and provisions for short term business visitors, with a view to possible improvements where this is in our mutual interest. 54. We intend to launch an EU-UK Digital Partnership early next year to enhance cooperation on digital and technology matters, in areas that could cover secure and resilient connectivity, artificial intelligence, including AI security and safety, critical technologies, including quantum, digital wallets and credentials, trust services, online safety and multilateral cooperation to deepen practical cooperation and to bring actions under a common structure. We consider it to be in our mutual interest to work together to ensure that our societies can take full advantage of the opportunities that science, research, technology and innovation provide, including their ability to safeguard our fundamental values and strengthening our democracies, while safeguarding our regulatory autonomy. This will help us drive innovation, strengthen trade, and benefit businesses and consumers alike. IV. Internal security and judicial cooperation 55. We recognise the value of the Trade and Cooperation Agreement and the Common Understanding in providing a valuable set of tools to facilitate our cooperation on matters related to law enforcement and judicial cooperation. We welcome the ongoing efforts to enhance cooperation on law enforcement and judicial cooperation in criminal matters with the aim of strengthening the security of both the EU and the UK. We welcome the signature of the Europol liaison officers arrangement and aim to continue to strengthen the UK’s relationship with Europol, recognising our strong existing operational cooperation. We also welcome the launch of the automated searching of vehicle registration data between the EU and the UK, which will render the work of law enforcement authorities more effective across borders. We also welcome continuous and strong cooperation between Eurojust and the UK authorities. We emphasise that further development of judicial cooperation is founded on the reciprocal and full implementation of the Trade and Cooperation Agreement and continued respect for the principles and commitments underpinning it. 56. The EU and the UK recognise the need for close coordination between the UK and the EU Member States on the removal of foreign national offenders. The UK and EU Member States commit to continue bilateral discussions, including on advance notification of such removals into each other’s territories on a reciprocal basis. We also refer to the possibility of encouraging further bilateral engagement on prisoner transfer cooperation, with a view to increasing the timeliness, efficiency and effectiveness of such cooperation. 57. We welcome the newly established cooperation between the EU and the UK on tackling the challenges related to drug trafficking and drug use, formalised through the signature of a working arrangement. 58. The EU and UK will explore the possible inclusion of the UK in the “Prüm international” initiative that the European Commission intends to present in mid-2027 to extend the Prüm framework on data exchange for police cooperation to chosen third country partners. 59. Recognising that the UK is a close partner, and in order to boost security and tackle irregular migration, the EU and the UK will also explore enhancing reciprocal information exchange for law enforcement and border management purposes. 60. We welcome and encourage continuing progress to overcome the difficulties that law enforcement and judicial authorities in one jurisdiction face in obtaining data from electronic service providers offering services in the other jurisdiction. We will continue exploring ways to reinforce mutual and reciprocal exchanges of data on criminal records of third country nationals, in the light of technical developments. V. Irregular migration 61. We welcome the deepened cooperation between the European Commission and the UK on the external dimension of migration. This includes regular information exchange on migration management projects, returns and visa related issues in respect of key countries of origin and transit relevant for irregular migration towards the EU and the UK. We aim to continue our cooperation, finding synergies in our engagement with partner countries and enhancing operational cooperation. 62. We will continue to pursue our cooperation in multinational fora, including in the context of the Global Alliance to Counter Migrant Smuggling, to promote our common values and interests and to partner for an effective management of global migration challenges. 63. We welcome the UK’s participation in the European Migration Network as an observer. This will strengthen exchanges of information and expertise on migration and asylum among the Network’s 35 members and observers. 64. We welcome the ongoing efforts by the European Union Agency for Asylum and the UK to work towards establishing a Working Arrangement to facilitate cooperation on asylum-related matters, in accordance with their respective mandates and legal frameworks and will pursue the discussions with a view to conclude them swiftly. We also welcome the continued cooperation between the UK and Frontex, in particular on risk analysis, information exchange, training and document fraud. 65. We welcome the UK’s participation in the Khartoum and Rabat processes. This will deepen our cooperation with countries of origin and transit, in particular along the Eastern, Central and Western Mediterranean and Atlantic routes. 66. In an era of increased security threats, cooperation between the EU and the UK is essential to address the shared challenges of irregular migration along the Channel and to prevent dangerous crossings. In this context, we welcome the adoption on 16 June 2026 of the European Commission’s Channel Action Plan, which sets forward a comprehensive framework for EU-level action and cooperation with the UK to tackle irregular migration and the criminal networks facilitating it as well as to strengthen border management. 67. We today commit to working closely together on joint activities under the Action Plan. This should include coordinated action to prevent and combat migrant smuggling and trafficking in human beings, including by disrupting the criminal supply chains underpinning them, addressing the drivers of irregular migration, preventing the misuse of legal migration channels and strengthening cooperation along key migratory routes. It should also enable work through relevant agencies, including Frontex, and more reciprocal information exchanges between interested EU Member States and the United Kingdom. Given the shared nature of these challenges, any new joint activities should be underpinned by a joint commitment, including, where appropriate, financial contributions, reflecting the shared roles and responsibilities for them. 68. Building on the implementation of the Channel Action Plan, the EU and UK will strengthen cooperation on shared migration challenges, taking a strategic, coordinated and whole-of-route approach, including through cooperation in priority third countries. To this end, they will establish a Structured Dialogue on migration covering in particular the joint activities under the Channel Action Plan, action against irregular migration and migrant smuggling networks, strategic communication and border management, upstream cooperation and engagement with third countries, returns to third countries, pull factors for irregular migrants and legal pathways. The Dialogue will also provide a framework for developing new ways to prevent and counter irregular migration, including through the exchange of best practices and operational cooperation, in accordance with national, EU and international law, respecting the respective competences of the Union and its Member States, and be based on mutual benefit and reciprocity. VI. Building a closer, more resilient partnership 69. Recognising the ties between the EU and the UK, we acknowledge our shared interest in building an even closer partnership. This partnership for economic resilience will be founded on our shared values, openness and democracy. It will be driven by the need to address our economic dependencies by building diversified, resilient supply chains through reciprocal market openness, mutual support and coordination on economic security, and developing a common prosperity and economic security space, with the principles of trust at its core. 70. As an immediate step, we will establish a Dialogue on Economic Security to coordinate our economic security policies. We will cooperate on export controls, on countering technology leakage in critical sectors, on mitigating risks to critical infrastructure, on resilient supply chains, including critical raw materials, tackling vulnerabilities and building on the complementarities of our economies, including early warning for supply disruptions. The objective of this coordination is to ensure a more effective and efficient response to our common challenges, for example by avoiding the circumvention of the measures we put in place to ensure the resilience of our economies. 71. Through this coordination and as a next step, the EU and the UK commit, on the basis of reciprocity, to strive, wherever possible, to limit negative effects on one another in their measures impacting specific supply chains. Under this partnership, where the EU and the UK agree to cooperate regarding a particular supply chain, the UK would ensure outcomes consistent with the relevant EU measures in order to ensure that the supply chain in question is protected in a consistent way across the EU and UK markets and guard against potential risks of circumvention. We will notably work towards diversified and resilient steel and electric vehicles supply chains, and emerging technologies together. The EU and the UK commit to taking work forward on this partnership as a matter of priority, and to review progress, in particular in these sectors, every four months. 72. We are putting this partnership into action already by providing our steel industries with the necessary protection against negative trade-related effects of overcapacity. We will explore further arrangements for addressing jointly the challenges and trade related negative effects of overcapacity. In light of the unique circumstances on the island of Ireland, recognising the existing solution under the Windsor Framework, a long-term sustainable solution for movement of UK originating steel to Northern Ireland would also be put in place.
